opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I don't think of it as three separate identities. The core of who I am professionally hasn't really changed: I'm someone who likes to find a problem that matters, dig into it deeply, and build something real that solves it.

In research, the goal is to push the frontier. You ask, "What's possible that nobody has shown yet?" You get to be very focused and very idealistic, and the reward is an insight or a system that changes how people think about a problem.

At a large company, the question shifts to "How does this work at scale, for real users, under real constraints?" That taught me a lot of humility. An idea that looks beautiful in a paper can fall apart when it meets production traffic, legacy systems, and organizational realities. I learned to care about reliability, cost, and the many unglamorous details that decide whether something actually gets used.

Starting a company combines both, plus a lot more. You still need the research mindset, because if you're not doing something technically differentiated, there's no reason for you to exist. You also need the engineering discipline from industry. On top of that, you have to think about customers, hiring, fundraising, and culture, which I was never trained for. So in some ways I feel like a beginner again, and I've learned to be comfortable with that.

If I had to name one identity, it would be "builder." Research, big tech, and a startup are just different environments for building, and each one taught me something the others couldn't. The biggest mental shift has been ownership. As a founder, there's no one else to hand a problem to. That's scary, but it's also the most motivating part.

r001.rationale: She describes herself as a builder who finds important problems and builds solutions, presenting her professional identity in service of that aim.

r002.rationale: She explains that research, large-company work, and founding each call for different supporting efforts—research insight, engineering discipline, and startup responsibilities—that contribute to building something useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, I've never thought of myself as having a fixed identity that changed when I moved from one setting to another. I think of it more as the same person applying the same curiosity to different problems, with different constraints.

When I was doing my PhD and then research at a large company, the identity was something like "I'm someone who finds hard technical problems and tries to solve them well." The problems were defined by what the field cared about and what the company needed. In research you optimize for a result that's new and that others can build on. At a big company you also optimize for things that will ship and that fit into a huge existing system. Both of those were genuinely satisfying, but you're always working inside a frame that someone else partly set.

Starting a company, the biggest shift for me wasn't going from researcher to "founder." It was that suddenly nobody else sets the frame. You have to decide what problem is worth working on, and you have to be honest about whether people actually want it, not just whether it's interesting. That's a different muscle. As a researcher you can fall in love with a clever idea. As a founder you have to be willing to let go of the clever idea if it doesn't serve the user.

But I'd say the core is continuous. A lot of what I did in open-source, like building systems that other people could actually run and depend on, was already halfway between research and product. People filed issues, they had real workloads, they told you when something broke. That taught me that the most meaningful technical work is the kind that lands in someone's hands. Starting a company is just taking that seriously as the main goal instead of a side effect.

So if I had to put a label on it today, I'd say I'm still an engineer and a researcher at heart. I just now also carry the responsibility of asking "who is this for, and why would they care?" before I ask "how do we make it fast?" And I actually think those questions make the technical work better, not worse.

r001.rationale: The response describes a continuous identity across roles and new founder responsibilities, but does not present identity as a means to accomplish what Ying Sheng wants to do.

r002.rationale: It describes distinct work across research, large-company engineering, and founding a company—such as pursuing novel results, shipping within existing systems, and validating user needs—as supporting meaningful technical work that reaches users.

astra-6.text:
I think of those as different ways of pursuing the same curiosity. In research, you’re asking, “Can this work?” At a large company, you also have to ask, “Can this work reliably, at scale?” And when you start a business, there’s another question: “Does this solve a problem that someone actually cares about?”

The biggest shift is in how I define progress. A technically interesting result can be valuable research, but it doesn’t automatically become a useful product. As a founder, you have to be willing to let what you learn from users change what you build.

So I don’t think you have to leave your identity as a researcher behind. You keep that habit of questioning assumptions and testing ideas. But you take on a broader responsibility for turning those ideas into something people can use.

r001.rationale: The response frames research, large-company work, and founding a business as different ways of pursuing the same curiosity, presenting professional identity as a means to pursue what she wants to do.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the work each path requires: testing whether something works, making it reliable at scale, and confirming it solves a problem users care about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of myself as someone who likes solving problems, and research, working at a large company, and starting a business are different ways of doing that. The biggest change is how you define the problem and what counts as success.

In research, you’re often asking, “Can we make this work?” At a large company, you also have to understand how your work fits into a bigger product and organization. As a founder, you have to ask an even more basic question: “Does anyone need this enough to use it or pay for it?” You’re responsible for finding the problem, building the solution, and making sure it reaches people.

So I don’t feel I have to leave the researcher identity behind. Curiosity and rigor are still valuable. But I do have to become more comfortable making decisions with incomplete information and learning directly from users. The technology is part of the answer; it’s no longer the whole answer.

r001.rationale: She describes herself as someone who likes solving problems and frames research, company work, and founding as different ways to do that.

r002.rationale: She explains that each path involves different work: testing whether something can work, fitting it into a product and organization, or validating demand and reaching users.
